newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia, Indonesia seen coal competitors.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia, Indonesia seen coal competitors.

text.p: Indonesia and Australia will become multi-billion dollar competitors in the booming Asian steaming coal market after a huge increase in coal mining investment in both countries into the first decade of the next century, an Australian coal conference was told on Tuesday.

Indonesian investment in coal production to year 2010 will outpip Australian investment at US$11.3 billion against Australia's $10.7 billion, according to projections presented to an APEC coal seminar by The Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics (ABARE).
China's investment in production of steaming coal -- used in power generation -- over the same period, between 1993 and 2010, is projected at a massive US$117.6 billion.
However, China's exports of steaming coal would not rise as greatly as Australia's or Indonesia's, ABARE said.
ABARE executive director Brian Fisher, in the keynote address to the conference, raised doubts about China's ability to effect the projected huge investment.

Indonesia and Australia are projected as the two dominant competitors in the APEC (Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation) region in the steaming coal export trade, predominantly for the Asian market, Fisher said.
According to ABARE, Australia will remain in the lead but feel stiffening Indonesian competition.
Australia's production of black steaming coal is projected to increase to 178.6 million tonnes in year 2010 from 104.3 million tonnes in 1992, a rise of about three percent a year.
Australian exports are projected to rise to 106.3 million tonnes from 58.3 million tonnes over the same period, an average annual increase of 3.4 percent.

Australia's investment requirements for steaming coal from the end of 1993 to the end of 2010 are estimated by ABARE at US$10.7 billion, while those for brown coal are estimated at $1.2 billion, giving a total investment of $11.9 billion.
Actual demand facing Australia will depend on policies in importing countries on the mix of alternative fuels, Fisher said. But he also sounded a warning for Australia about Indonesian competition.
"Export demand for Australian coal could be affected by Indonesian policies which could markedly affect domestic demand and influence Indonesian exports," Fisher said.
The ABARE projections show Indonesia exporting 64.9 million tonnes of steam coal by year 2010.
It is possible that Indonesian exports may be constrained to 45 million tonnes by limited reserves of high quality steaming coal, Fisher said.
But very ambitious Indonesian plans for domestic consumption could see investment requirements for steaming coal production rising to US$15.9 billion from 1993 to 2010, he said.
